loc_385.loc_89: Ocean circulation changes rather than global warming drove temperature trends across the Miocene Climatic Optimum

loc_365.loc_110: Evi Wubben 1 †, Xiaoqing Liu 2 *†, Tjerk J. T. Veenstra 1 , R. Paul Acosta 3 , Joyce den Hollander 1 , Chris Overduin 1 , Matthew Huber 2 , Francesca Sangiorgi 1 , Francien Peterse 1 , Appy Sluijs 1

loc_397.loc_194: Early-­to-­Middle Miocene [23 to 13.8 million years ago (Ma)] climates were ∼6° to 9°C warmer than today. Around 16.9 Ma, benthic foraminiferal oxygen isotope (δ 18 O) records suggest pronounced warming, known as the Miocene Climatic Optimum (MCO) onset. However, explaining this putative global warming with carbon dioxide (CO2) forcing faces challenges in terms of timing and forcing magnitude. Our new biomarker-­based ocean temperature records, combined with published data, reveal no substantial mean global upper ocean warming across the MCO. Instead, temperature changes differ considerably between sites, with some regions showing cooling. Climate model sensitivity tests indicate that these patterns are best explained by ocean circulation changes, likely due to gateway changes and Antarctic ice sheet variations. This suggests that the MCO signature is better attributed to ocean circulation changes rather than a CO2-­driven global warming event. The δ 18 O signal therefore represents warmer deepwater sourcing and/or reduced Antarctic glacial volume, resolving the longstanding challenge of explaining MCO warming without a pronounced CO2 rise.

loc_245.loc_308: During the Early-­to-­Middle Miocene [23 to 13.8 million years ago (Ma)], reconstructed atmospheric CO2 concentrations ranged from 400 to 600 parts per million (ppm) (1), similar to contemporary CO2 levels and those projected for the near future (2). Multiproxy reconstructions of bottom water temperature (BWT) and sea surface temperature (SST) suggest generally warmer conditions during this period, with average BWTs of 5° to 9°C (3, 4) and SSTs of 7° to 8°C higher than the present-­day (5, 6). Therefore, this period, including the Miocene Climatic Optimum (MCO; 16.9 to 14.5 Ma), provides a useful analog for the future (5). A fundamental understanding of temperature changes and their drivers during this interval helps us evaluate climate model performance and, thus, improve projections of future temperature responses to CO2 changes (7).

loc_469.loc_131: The MCO onset is typically identified by an abrupt ∼1 per mil (‰) drop in deep ocean benthic foraminifer oxygen isotope ratios (δ 18 Obenthic) from 17 to 16.8 Ma (8), which is interpreted as deep ocean warming (9-11). The generalized relationship between δ 18 Obenthic and global mean surface temperature suggests ∼2.7°C of global surface warming across the MCO onset (12), which forms the basis for the term MCO. However, the few existing SST and BWT reconstructions across the MCO show ambiguous warming signatures (11, 13-17). In contrast, abrupt changes in δ 18 Obenthic across the onset of the Paleocene-­Eocene Thermal Maximum [>10 thousand years (kyr)], during glacial expansion recorded by the earliest Oligocene oxygen isotope step (∼40 kyr), and through Pleistocene last deglaciations (∼8 kyr) are supported by corresponding changes in SST proxy records (18-20). loc_470.loc_337: Warming across the MCO onset has been attributed to rising atmospheric CO2 concentrations due to CO2 degassing from Columbia River Basalt Group (CRBG) (21, 22). However, if global warming comprised close to 3°C as might be derived from the deep ocean δ 18 Obenthic record, then it is difficult to reconcile with the moderate CO2 increase of ∼100 to 150 ppm, from ∼400 ppm between 19 and 17 Ma to ∼520 ppm between 16.9 and 15.5 Ma, estimated from multiple proxy records recently evaluated by the CenCO2PIP Consortium (1) and a recent reconstruction (23). Also, carbon-­cycle simulations (24) incorporating CO2 outgassing from CRBG indicate a CO2 rise of 90 to 100 ppm across the MCO onset (25, 26). Collectively, considering the apparent spatial heterogeneity in surface temperature trends and evidence for only a small rise in atmospheric pCO2, we hypothesize that the onset of the MCO does not represent a global surface warming phase but rather a large-­scale change in surface heat distribution.

loc_470.loc_431: Change in ocean heat distribution may arise from tectonic forcing, particularly the opening and closing of oceanic gateways. Such changes are typically difficult to date with the precision needed to link them to astronomically dated climate events, such as the onset of the MCO. However, several important tectonic changes appear to roughly coincide with this time interval, including the deepening of the Greenland-­Scotland Ridge (GSR) (27), the closure of the Central American Seaway (CAS) (28), and the shallowing of the Tethys Seaway (29, 30). These processes may have altered regional ocean heat transport. In addition, the Antarctic ice sheet (AIS) retreated substantially during the MCO (31-35), which, according to model simulations, might have contributed to regional surface warming and cooling (7, 36-38).

loc_470.loc_68: Here, we test whether the MCO represents a global warming phase or, alternatively, a major reorganization of ocean circulation driven by tectonic changes. We first improve spatial coverage of temperature records across the MCO by selecting sites from northern mid-­ and high latitudes, tropical regions, and southern mid-­ and high latitudes (Fig. 1). Constraints on global mean upper ocean and surface temperature changes across the MCO require high-­resolution ocean temperature records. We recently published a high-­resolution ocean temperature record based on the TetraEther indeX of 86 carbon atoms [TEX86; (39)] from Ocean Drilling Program (ODP) Site 959 in the eastern equatorial Atlantic, which effectively resolves orbital-­ scale variability (11). Although this proxy has certain limitations (40) (Supplementary Text), it is valuable because, unlike the alkenone unsaturation index (U k′ 37) (41), it retains sensitivity at temperatures beyond the modern ocean range, an essential requirement for reconstructing ocean temperature variability in the tropical belt during the Miocene (5). In addition, it is not affected by diagenesis like biogenic calcite-­based proxies (42) and can be applied in most marine settings. Here, we add new high-­resolution TEX86-­based ocean temperature records covering the MCO from ODP Site 1007 (average resolution, ∼15 kyr) at the Great Bahama Bank in the western tropical Atlantic, ODP Site 643 (∼180 kyr) in the Norwegian Sea, and ODP Site 1165 (∼70 kyr) offshore Prydz Bay, Antarctica, including updated age models for Sites 1007 and 1165 (figs. S1 and S2). We also present lower-­resolution temperature records based on TEX86 and U k′ 37 from seven more sites to extend stratigraphic ranges of published records and to improve spatial coverage in the equatorial Pacific and southern mid-­latitude Pacific Ocean (Fig. 1, table S1, and fig. S3). To account for the depth derivation of TEX86 signals, we here explicitly treat TEX86 as a proxy for integrated upper ocean temperature (40). Based on these new TEX86 and U k′ 37 records, together with previously published TEX86, U k′ 37, planktonic foraminiferal Mg/Ca ratios, and clumped isotope (Δ47) records (tables S1 and S2 and figs. S4 to S6), we estimate global mean upper ocean and surface temperature changes and quantify the spatial pattern of upper ocean temperature shifts during the MCO.

loc_470.loc_148: Second, we explore the underlying mechanisms driving temperature variability by comparing reconstructed patterns with simulated ocean temperature changes driven by variations in atmospheric CO2 concentrations, oceanic gateways, and the AIS. loc_470.loc_221: We convert TEX86 values to shallow subsurface temperature (SubT) using two calibrations that together encompass the plausible range of the proxy response to temperature: one integrating the top 200 m of the water column (SubT0-­200) (46), and the other integrating depths between 100 and 250 m (SubT100-­250) (47), representing a more conservative proxy response (Materials and Methods).

loc_245.loc_134: Our new SubT records from ODP Sites 643, 1007, and 1165 (Fig. 2), as well as our seven new low-­resolution SubT and SST records (fig. S3), show diverging Early-­to-­Middle Miocene temperature trends. At Site 643 (Fig. 2A), warming occurs in the interval before the MCO (∼18 to 17.5 Ma), with an increase of ∼3°C in SubT0-­200 (∼2.5°C in SubT100-­250). This warming contrasts with a concomitant cooling trend recorded at two other North Atlantic sites, Sites 982 and 608 (Fig. 2A). The pre-­MCO warming at Site 643 is of greater magnitude than the ∼2.5°C increase in SubT0-­200 (∼2°C in SubT100-­250) across the MCO onset at ∼16.9 Ma, during which Site 982 shows a ∼2°C increase in SubT0-­200, and Site 608 does not exhibit a notable change. At Site 643, peak SubT values at ∼17 Ma are followed by a transient cooling of ∼3.5°C (∼3°C with SubT100-­250) between ∼16.5 and 15.5 Ma, but the average SubT during the MCO (∼17 to 14 Ma) remains elevated compared with the pre-­MCO by ∼1°C.

loc_245.loc_235: No warming is recorded at the MCO onset at Site 1007 (Fig. 2). Instead, a ∼2.5°C warming (∼2°C with SubT100-­250) is recorded from ∼17.6 to 17.4 Ma, leading to peak SubTs between 17.4 and 17 Ma, similar to Site 643. However, unlike Site 643, temperatures at Site 1007 decrease between ∼17 and 16.5 Ma, returning to levels of before 17.5 Ma. At both sites, elevated temperatures occurred again between ∼15.5 and 15 Ma. Similar to a previous record (11), these temperature peaks may reflect the ∼400-­kyr eccentricity maximum during this period. The records of pre-­MCO warming could be related to a pCO2 increase that preconditioned the drop in δ 18 Obenthic, but they might also reflect regional trends because not all SST and SubT records show pre-­MCO warming. Moreover, current compilations, albeit of low resolution, do not indicate such a CO2 rise preceding the MCO (Fig. 2B).

loc_245.loc_381: At Site 1165, across the δ 18 Obenthic negative excursion interval from 17 to 16.8 Ma at the onset of the MCO, a slight cooling of ∼1.7°C (∼1.4°C with SubT100-­250) occurs from 17.1 to 16.7 Ma, followed by an abrupt and transient warming of ∼5.8°C (∼4.9°C with SubT100-­250) at ∼16.77 Ma, reflected in a single data point. This warming is immediately followed by a cooling of ∼9.5°C (∼8°C with SubT100-­250) from ∼16.77 to 16.74 Ma (Fig. 2). These abrupt warming and cooling events invite even higher-­resolution TEX86 data and a refined age model for evaluation of consistency. After ∼16.7 Ma, SubT changes exhibit short-­scale (∼100 to 500 kyr) variability with an amplitude of ∼4° to 6°C (∼3° to 5°C SubT100-­250) (Fig. 2A), which may represent the influence of orbital insolation variations. For reconstructions of SubT variability at potentially cold, high-­latitude sites, a recently proposed index that includes hydroxylated isoprenoid GDGTs (OH-­GDGTs) may be more suitable (48) (Materials and Methods). TEX86 OH -­based SubTs from ODP Sites 643 and 1165 show similar trends as those based on TEX86 (fig. S8). While the two indices provide similar absolute SubTs at Site 643, absolute SubTs at Site 1165 are, on average, 7°C lower with TEX86 OH -­SubT than with TEX86 SubT0-­200, and variability is slightly reduced.

loc_245.loc_468: To evaluate globally averaged temperature change across the MCO onset (∼16.9 Ma), we compile published SubT and SST records spanning the Early Miocene (19 to 17 Ma) and MCO (16.9 to 14 Ma) (tables S1 and S2). Like our new records, published SST and SubT records show ambiguous temperature trends across the MCO onset (figs. S6 and S8), with some records indicating warming, whereas others show no change or changes at different time intervals. Using these SST and SubT records from 28 sites, we calculate anomalies relative to modern values at each site (Fig. 3) and then determine globally weighted mean SST (GMSST) and SubT (GMSubT) anomalies

loc_472.loc_104: (Table 1) using a conventional approach based on tropical, mid-­ latitude, and high-­latitude temperature anomalies (49). We then compare global mean SST/SubT anomalies for the pre-­MCO (19 to 17 Ma) and the early phase of the MCO (16.9 to 15.5 Ma) relative to the modern (Fig. 4A and Table 1). Additionally, because the late phase of the MCO (15.5 to 14 Ma) was somewhat cooler than the early phase in some records (11, 50), we investigate whether this cooling represents a global trend by comparing global mean SST/SubT anomalies between the two intervals (Fig. 4C and Table 1).

loc_470.loc_221: From the pre-­MCO to the first stage of the MCO, the GMSST anomaly increases from ∼8.2° to ∼9.6°C, but this rise is insignificant because the error on both estimates approximates this signal (Table 1). SST warming is most prominent in the mid-­latitudes (∼2.1°C ΔSSTanomaly), whereas high-­latitude SST shows no detectable change (-0.8°C ΔSSTanomaly; Fig. 4A), albeit only based on a single record (Site 643). In contrast, the GMSubT change, as well as SubT changes across low, mid-­, and high latitudes, is negligible (Fig. 4A). Evidently, there is no systematic warming of the global surface ocean at the MCO onset as defined by the drop in δ 18 Obenthic, in contrast to the consistent global ocean warming across the Paleocene-­Eocene Thermal Maximum (18) or Pleistocene deglaciations (20, 51, 52). Collectively, this nonuniform warming pattern suggests that changes in ocean circulation patterns, potentially with additional feedbacks from ice sheet retreats (37, 53), and resulting changes in heat distributions played a more important role than atmospheric CO2 forcing.

loc_472.loc_300: The GMSST and GMSubT changes, as well as SST and SubT changes in low, mid-­, and high latitudes (Fig. 4B), from the pre-­MCO (19 to 17 Ma) to the late phase of the MCO (15.5 to 14 Ma), exhibit similar patterns to those from the pre-­MCO to the early MCO (Fig. 4A). This is indicated by no significant difference between the late and early MCO SST/SubT anomalies (Fig. 4C), except for high-­ latitude SubTs, where the late MCO is slightly cooler than the early phase (Fig. 4C). Similar to the warming at the onset of the MCO, not all sites within a single latitudinal band exhibit consistent SST trends toward the late MCO; some sites show warming, whereas others show cooling relative to pre-­MCO conditions.

loc_245.loc_315: The spatial heterogeneity across the MCO is unlikely to be caused by CO2 changes alone as CO2 increases lead to a more globally uniform warming pattern (Fig. 6C). It is also unlikely that this heterogeneity was caused by the closure of the CAS or the shallowing of the Tethys Seaway as the resulting pattern of SubT changes (Fig. 6, E and F) does not match the reconstructed pattern. The warming at North Atlantic Site 643 may result from the deepening of the GSR (Fig. 6D), where tectonic phases occurred from the Eocene to the Miocene (56, 57). However, this warming would likely be offset by cooling linked to the closure of the CAA gateway (Fig. 6G) if the deepening of the GSR and the closure of the CAA gateway occurred simultaneously, although the combined response could differ from the sum of their individual effects because of nonlinear interactions. In addition, cooling in the North Atlantic at Site 982 during the second phase of the MCO and at Site 608 during both phases of the MCO, together with the warming in the tropical Atlantic (Site 959) and southern mid-­latitudes (Sites 516 and 1168), can be attributed to the closure of the CAA gateway (Fig. 6G). The Antarctic cooling at Site 1165 is similar to that resulting from the AIS retreat (Fig. 6H), whereas the cooling at another Antarctic site, AND-­2A in the Ross Sea region (Fig. 6B), contrasts with the modeled warming of ∼0.5°C. The reconstructed cooling of ∼0.5°C at the second phase of the MCO is estimated from five data points clustered around 14.5 Ma (Fig. 5G) and may therefore be biased by limited sampling. Sediment lithology at AND-­2A, notably evidence for more frequent open water conditions and larger distance from ice, rather supports warmer conditions during the MCO (58). Moreover, as TEX86 is related to lithology in this record (58), selecting samples in a certain lithology can potentially introduce bias into reconstructed temperatures. At Site 1165, such relations still require further investigation. The TEX86 records from the Antarctic margin should thus be interpreted with caution. Additionally, the simulated temperature change likely depends on the ice sheet geometry, which, in (36), follows an idealized, sea level-adjusted ice volume and does not account for possible shifts in ice sheet areal extent. In summary, the reconstructed patterns of SubT changes are broadly consistent with changes in oceanic gateways, particularly the deepening of the GSR and the closure of the CAA gateway, as well as AIS retreat.

loc_470.loc_133: Because no individual forcing experiment reproduces the entire reconstructed spatial pattern, we next explore whether a combination of these forcings provides a closer match. In the absence of multiforcing simulations, we assign different scaling factors to the temperature responses simulated in the individual forcing experiments as a first-­order device for testing pattern consistency. This exercise is inherently artificial because it necessarily assumes that the responses to individual forcings can be combined linearly. In reality, the climatic response to multiple gateway depth changes is strongly nonlinear and region dependent (59, 60). Accordingly, the assigned scaling factors should not be interpreted as physics-­based estimates of the actual magnitude of gateway or AIS changes or their respective climatic contributions. Rather, the purpose of this calculation is solely to demonstrate that only a combination of forcings can reproduce, or at least more closely approach, the proxy-­derived spatial pattern. We present two combinations that align well with it. "Combination I" (Fig. 6I) includes twice the temperature change caused by the deepening of the GSR (Fig. 6D), one-­fourth of the temperature change caused by the closure of the CAA gateway (Fig. 6G), and twice the temperature change caused by the AIS retreat (Fig. 6H). "Combination II" (Fig. 6J) builds on Combination I, adding one-­fourth of the temperature change resulting from a CO2 increase from 400 to 560 ppm (Fig. 6C). Both combinations show a strong correlation with the reconstructed spatial pattern (Fig. 6, A and B), with centered pattern correlation coefficients ranging from 0.7 to 0.8. These correlations illustrate consistency in the direction and spatial structure of temperature change, although the optimal combination that best matches the proxy pattern may not correspond to the scaling factors assigned here. Nonetheless, they support our main point that a combination of these physical forcings produces the proxy-­based pattern of SubT changes. In addition, SST changes from combinations I and II match the direction of U k′ 37-­based SST changes (table S3) at three open-­ocean sites (Sites 884, 982, and 1168) (fig. S10), although the magnitudes of SST changes are not consistent.

loc_470.loc_410: In our simulations, the warming in the Norwegian Sea caused by the deepening of the GSR in our CESM simulations results from an enhanced flux of subtropical water, both within and below the mixed layer, into the Norwegian Sea along the eastern boundary (fig. S17). Cooling recorded south of the GSR (Site 982) is caused by an increased flux of cold Arctic-­origin water (including from the Norwegian Sea) into the northern North Atlantic along the western boundary, compared with the control experiment, in which the GSR acts as a barrier that restricts water mass exchange between the Norwegian Sea and the northern North Atlantic (fig. S17). Although deepening of the GSR during the Miocene has been linked to enhanced export of North Atlantic Deep Water (NADW) (27, 61, 62) to the Atlantic Ocean and a potential intensification of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC), neither our control nor deep-­GSR experiments show NADW formation (fig. S18, A to D), and deepening of the GSR has little impact on AMOC strength in our simulations (fig. S18, E to G). In contrast, the closure of the CAA reduces the AMOC strength and northward Atlantic Ocean heat transport, leading to cooling in the North Atlantic and south of the Norwegian Sea, as well as warming in the tropical Atlantic (Fig. 6G) (45). AIS retreat induces changes in the deep-­water formation in the Weddell and Ross Seas, leading to strong cooling in the Atlantic-­Indian sector of the Southern Ocean and moderate warming in the Ross Sea region (37). In addition, AIS-­ocean feedback may contribute to regional temperature changes, i.e., AIS retreat could induce positive feedbacks, leading to weaker southward heat transport and localized high-­latitude cooling, which, in turn, reorganizes ocean circulation (53). The negative cloud feedback associated with AIS retreat also contributes to regional ocean surface cooling (37, 53). One caveat of these explanations is that the resolution of the ocean model may not adequately resolve regional circulation patterns. Improved ocean circulation resulting from increased model resolution (63) could also provide an alternative explanation for the observed spatial heterogeneity, warranting further investigation.

loc_245.loc_75: Although the spatial fingerprint of MCO temperature changes can be plausibly linked to alterations in ocean circulation caused by the deepening of the GSR and the closure of the CAA, combined with a retreat of the AIS, the question may rise whether this forcing scenario itself is plausible. Current tectonic data cannot date oceanic gateway changes with the precision needed to test our forcing hypothesis. However, model experiments suggest that even modest bathymetric shifts, when near a threshold state, can drive large circulation changes (27, 64), heat transport, and cloud feedbacks, leading to changes in regional ocean temperatures as described above. At the very least, the tectonic forcing proposed here provides the best explanation to date for the recorded temperature changes across the MCO.

loc_245.loc_206: Although CO2 changes were not the primary driver of SST changes across the MCO, an increase in atmospheric CO2 levels during this period may have contributed to the reconstructed warming at some sites and to a GMSST rise smaller than our errors (Table 1). However, the magnitude of CO2 rise was likely relatively small: as an increase of 160 ppm (from 400 to 560 ppm) simulates a warming 1.5 to 2 times greater than reconstructed at our study sites (Fig. 6C). Any CO2 increase was therefore probably smaller than the ∼150-­ppm increase from pre-­MCO to early MCO derived by CenCO2PIP (1), which is largely based on boron isotopes. This interpretation is also supported by independent evidence from algal 13 C-­fractionation, which suggests a CO2 increase of only 100 to 150 ppm across the MCO onset (23). Even a small increase in CO2 may nonetheless have contributed to the retreat of the AIS, due to its highly dynamic and variable response to relatively modest CO2 changes (31, 58). Additional high-­resolution CO2 records, particularly those based on proxies other than boron isotopes, are needed to better constrain CO2 variability across the MCO.

loc_470.loc_53: Our data indicate that GMSST warming across the MCO was negligible. The estimated ratio of GMSST changes to deep ocean temperature changes for the Cenozoic, ranges from 0.46 to 0.87 (12). This might suggest that MCO warming in the deep ocean was also negligible. However, the coupling between GMSST changes to deep ocean temperature is typically attributed to greenhouse forcing (12, 65). In this case, the recorded ocean circulation change might have warmed regions of deepwater formation, leading to deep ocean warming without pronounced GMSST rise. The clumped isotope-­based deep ocean temperature records may have insufficient information, notably in the pre-­MCO interval, to test this hypothesis (Fig. 2D) (66-69). Regardless, the ∼0.5‰ drop in δ 18 Obenthic across the MCO (Fig. 2C) could represent a drop in seawater δ 18 O (δ 18 Osw) due to a decrease in global ice volume. Process modeling with the δ 18 Obenthic stack shows a eustatic rise of ∼15 m at the onset of the MCO, accompanied by a deep sea warming of ∼1.2°C (70). If less of the δ 18 Obenthic signal during the MCO represents deep ocean warming, then the sea level rise must have been larger. A Cenozoic sea level estimate based on deep-­sea geochemical records (71) indicates a 30-­ to 40-­m sea level rise across the MCO (Fig. 2E), but discussion on the magnitude of eustatic variability in this record continues. Isotope-­enabled models of the AIS simulate an ice volume decrease equivalent to a 30-­ to 36-­m sea level change, which amounts to a ∼0.5 to 0.7‰ decrease in δ 18 O of seawater (31). Proxy records show that the AIS was highly dynamic during the MCO, even retreating to a land-­ based ice sheet (32, 33, 72), which might support a large change. Deciphering the factors initiating AIS retreat is challenging because of the complex interactions among ocean circulation, wind fields, and the sea-­ice system (37): The AIS retreat could have been triggered by even modest pCO2 increases, given the high sensitivity of the AIS to pCO2 (31, 58), combined with subsequent feedbacks involving ocean circulation changes (73, 74), winds, and sea-­ice dynamics. Collectively, the lack of pronounced GMSST and GMSubT warming across the MCO suggests a dynamic AIS and that existing analyses based on δ 18 Obenthic underestimate the ice sheet response during the MCO.

loc_470.loc_184: In summary, the now available data, including our new Miocene marine temperature records and published records, indicate limited global mean warming across the MCO onset (∼16.9 Ma). Additionally, the direction and magnitude of upper ocean and surface temperature changes during the MCO are highly variable between regions. Based on a large set of coupled climate model simulations, we find that this heterogeneity can be satisfactorily explained by changes in ocean circulation and subsequent shifts in ocean heat transport caused by the closure of the CAA, the deepening of the GSR, and the retreat of the AIS, and not primarily by CO2 forcing. This finding represents an important advance in demonstrating that the spatial pattern of ocean temperature changes across the MCO is better explained by a combination of regional paleogeographic changes superimposed on global ocean circulation changes and elevated pCO2, rather than by pCO2 alone. Future work using large-­ensemble approaches with systematically varied combinations of boundary conditions will be needed to more robustly quantify the nonlinear interactions and constrain the mechanisms driving ocean temperature changes across the MCO.
